tagline.text: Open-air pools of 40°C water in the rainforest at the foot of Mount Hibok-Hibok

location.label: Location
location.text: Esperanza Tagdo, Mambajao, Camiguin, at the foot of Mount Hibok-Hibok

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱30–500 (entrance, shed and snacks, excluding transport)

children.text: Ardent Hot Spring is an open-air hot spring in the forest at the foot of the active volcano Mount Hibok-Hibok in Mambajao, Camiguin. Water of about 40°C flows down through several pools, making it a good place to ease your muscles after a day out, and the entrance fee is low.

Ardent Hot Spring is an open-air hot spring at the foot of the active volcano Mount Hibok-Hibok in Mambajao, on Camiguin island. According to one travel blog, Camiguin has seven volcanoes, which is why hot and cold springs rise all over the island, and Ardent is one of the springs visitors go to most. It is about a 10-minute drive from central Mambajao, and a location site says it lies about 3.2 km in a straight line from Camiguin Airport, about 4.3 km from the Provincial Capitol and about 3.1 km from a point on Mount Hibok-Hibok. If you stay in Mambajao on the north of the island, it is easy to fit into your plans.
The spring is built as several man-made pools (described as four or six, depending on the source) that collect water coming down from a valley above. One guide says the water is about
at the source and cools slightly toward the lower pools. The two large pools at the bottom are the most popular and are linked by an arched footbridge, with a depth of about
and concrete steps around the edges. The water is clear with a tinge of blue, and the setting is surrounded by rainforest.

Facilities are simple. Sheds and tables around the edge of the spring can be rented, and a small cafe sells local dishes, drinks and snacks. The name includes the word resort, and it is known to have had bungalow-style rooms and a camping area for a long time, but most pricing information comes from posts more than ten years old, so the current situation is hard to confirm. For that reason, it is more realistic to visit for a short soak in the daytime or evening than to stay overnight. According to a 2025 guide, it is open daily from
to
, and on Wednesday mornings the pools are drained for cleaning and hard to use. Hours may change, so check before you go.

Visitor reviews are mixed. One blogger who went at night wrote that the music was too loud, the area around the pools was very slippery and the lighting was dim, while another guide recommends it for easing sore muscles after a full day of sightseeing. Either way, because the entrance fee is cheap and access is easy, you will be less disappointed if you think of it as a neighborhood hot spring that local families enjoy rather than a glamorous spa. To sum up, Ardent Hot Spring is less a must-see on a Camiguin itinerary than a supporting stop to end the day. Added as an evening after a daytime tour of waterfalls, beaches, the Sunken Cemetery and White Island, it adds little travel and costs the least. If you would rather find a quiet, clean spring, pick a weekday daytime or early evening and manage your expectations about the slippery floor and the music.
The water at the source is known to be about
, and it flows from top to bottom into several pools (one source gives about 33–40°C across the pools). It is fun to move between the two large lower pools and compare temperatures.
An arched bridge stands between the two large pools at the bottom, a good spot for photos. The water is clear enough to show a blue tinge, and the surroundings are rainforest.

blocks.title: At the foot of Mount Hibok-Hibok

children.text: It lies at the foot of Mount Hibok-Hibok (about
), Camiguin's best-known active volcano, so you get the most direct feeling of a volcanic hot spring. Many travelers combine it with a climb of the same mountain on one day.
Two 2026 sources agree on ₱30 for adults (₱15 for children), while some tour pages quote ₱50. Cash only, so check on site. Recent posts say sheltered tables and chairs cost an extra ₱150 or so.
Because it stays open late, you can soak after dark. One blogger wrote that most visitors go at night. Be careful, though, because the lighting is dim and the floor is slippery.
A small cafe inside the resort sells local dishes, drinks and snacks. Menu prices were not confirmed, so ask on site.

blocks.title: A closing stop on a Camiguin island tour

children.text: It is often suggested as a closing stop for an evening soak after a tour around the island. It suits travelers with tight muscles especially well.

A 2013 post gives fast craft fares of ₱550–750 and some older posts around ₱150, so fares vary widely by period and vessel. Check the current fare before you travel.

You can use the hot spring year-round, so the season does not matter much. For a Camiguin trip as a whole, one guide says November to March is the easiest, with less rain and cooler weather. April to July is hot and dry but peak season and crowded, and August to October is typhoon season, which the guide advises avoiding.

Within the week, it is best to avoid weekends. One guide wrote that weekends are very crowded with local families. One blogger says the pools are emptied and cleaned on Wednesday mornings, so avoid that time.

Accommodation on Camiguin is concentrated in Mambajao and nearby beaches, so staying in Mambajao is convenient for this spring. One guide lists the five-star Bintana Sa Paraiso in Mambajao as high-end, Tongatok Cliff Resort as mid-range and Pabua's Cottages as a budget choice. The hot spring resort itself is known to have cottage-style and dormitory-style rooms, but current prices could not be confirmed.

You can eat a simple meal at the small cafe in the spring. A reasonable order is to have a proper meal in central Mambajao and drop in for a soak afterward. Check that seafood is fresh with your own eyes and ask the price first. Central Mambajao has restaurants and shops that are convenient to visit before or after the spring, and the cafe's menu prices have to be checked on site.
Shed fees differ by source, so check on site. Adult entrance is most often given as ₱30 (child ₱15); some sources say ₱50.
Weekends are crowded with local families. Go on a weekday if you can.
The pools are reportedly drained and cleaned on Wednesday mornings, so avoid that time.
The area around the pools and bridge is very slippery. Wear non-slip sandals and walk slowly.
The lighting is dim at night. Bring a small flashlight or use your phone's light.
The music tends to be loud, so it may not suit anyone expecting quiet relaxation.
Bring a towel, a change of clothes and a waterproof bag, and leave valuables at your accommodation.
The area around the pools is very slippery and dark at night. One visitor wrote that several people slipped and a companion sprained an ankle. Walk slowly.
Facility fees (sheds, tables and so on) differ among posts, so they need to be checked locally.
The water is about 40°C. If you have high blood pressure or a heart condition, or are pregnant, do not soak for long and consult a doctor first.
Soaking after drinking alcohol is dangerous. Avoid it especially in the dark at night.
On Wednesday mornings, when the pools are cleaned, use may not be possible.
This is a volcanic area, so check conditions at Mount Hibok-Hibok and PHIVOLCS advisories before you leave.
An introduction to the whole island and how to get around is in the island's own entry. The spring is on the Mambajao side in the north of the island.
A sandbar about 2 km off the northern coast of Mambajao, with a pump boat at about ₱550 and an entrance fee of about ₱50. It combines well with the hot spring on the same day.
